title: Knowledge check: Working with Basic Expressions

questions.prompt: For “Working with Basic Expressions”, which approach best supports a reliable result?
options: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
Trust the first output without inspecting its inputs.
Hide warnings and skip validation to make the result look clean.
Change several unrelated parts at once so the cause of any result is unclear.
questions.answer_key: Inspect assumptions, run a small example, and verify an edge case.
questions.explanation: Working with Basic Expressions is one step in Data Types, Values, and Basic Objects; r objects have types and classes. Missingness (NA), undefined numeric results (NaN), infinities, and NULL are distinct. Reliable work makes assumptions visible and checks behavior before scaling up.

questions.prompt: Which item is explicitly listed under “Working with Basic Expressions” in the source curriculum?
options: Change unrelated settings before checking the input
Assume one example proves every edge case
Skip validation when the output looks plausible
questions.explanation: The source PDF lists “Creating Expressions” as part of lesson 27. The lesson retains the original topic wording.

questions.prompt: When applying “Working with Basic Expressions” to real work, what should you do before relying on the result?
options: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
Assume missing and malformed inputs never occur.
Use the same method regardless of data type or the research question.
Remove inconvenient observations without recording the decision.
questions.answer_key: Validate inputs and output shape, test a boundary case, and state limitations.
questions.explanation: Inspect with str(), typeof(), class(), is.na(), and explicit assertions before transforming data. Record assumptions and known limitations instead of presenting a demonstration as proof.
